Lesson 01

Run a model locally when the data should stay put

Why it matters

Local is a privacy and latency choice. It is not automatically the more accurate choice.

Try it: Memory fit

Lesson
01 of 07
Time
11 min
Level
Core
Local means
You control the machine
It does not mean
More accurate
Still
Pin the id

A local model runs on hardware you control. The prompt does not leave the machine, unless the software you wrapped around it sends it somewhere. That is the reason to prefer local for private notes, drafts of unreleased work, and air-gapped labs.

Accuracy is a separate question. A small local model can lose to a frontier API on hard reasoning and still be the right tool, because the task is simple enough and the data cannot move. Measure both. Do not treat 'local' as a moral category or 'cloud' as one.

Choose local whenChoose a hosted API when
The text is private and you have no approval to send it.The task fails on the local model and the data is allowed to move.
You need to work offline.You need a frontier or reasoning model you cannot fit.
You want a fixed, repeatable lab.You want capacity on demand and will pay per token.

Practice

Write one task that must stay on the machine and one task you would send to an API if the data were allowed to move. Name the reason in a clause, not a slogan.

Check

Does local mean more accurate?

Show the answer

No. It means you control where the weights run and where the prompt goes. Accuracy is an eval result.

Lesson 02

Install a runner and call it on localhost

Why it matters

Ollama and llama.cpp are the usual local runners. The smoke check is a local HTTP call or a CLI completion.

Try it: Memory fit

Lesson
02 of 07
Time
13 min
Level
Core
Runners
Ollama or llama.cpp
Listen on
Localhost
Smoke
One short prompt

Two common runners in 2026 are Ollama, which gives you a local service and a simple CLI, and llama.cpp, which runs GGUF weights with fine control over hardware. LM Studio and MLX on Apple silicon are other local options. vLLM is what teams use when they serve an open model to many callers. You do not need all of them.

A first path

  1. Install one runner from its official site or package.
  2. Pull a small instruct model whose license you have read.
  3. Confirm the process is listening only on localhost if you use HTTP.
  4. Send one short prompt at low temperature.
  5. Save the model id and the raw response as the artifact.
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags

That call lists models on a local Ollama. It is not required to study this page.
If nothing is listening, the correct result is a connection error, which you record.

No runner yet

Keep going. Later practices accept a written plan in place of a live call. Do not create an API key just to finish a local-model lesson.

Practice

If a runner is installed, save the tag list or the CLI's model list. If not, write the runner you will install and the exact check you will use to prove it is up.

Check

Where should a personal lab listen?

Show the answer

On localhost. A model service bound to every network interface is a different, riskier setup.

Lesson 03

Pick a model size that fits in memory

Why it matters

If the weights do not fit, the runner will swap, crash, or refuse. Start smaller than your pride.

Try it: Memory fit

Lesson
03 of 07
Time
11 min
Level
Practice
Limit
Memory, not the slogan
16 GB start
7B or 8B, Q4 or Q5
Then
One size up after smoke

Memory is the constraint, not the slogan on the model card. A quantized 7B or 8B instruct model is a common first fit on a 16 GB laptop. Machines with 8 GB should start smaller. A 32 GB machine can try a larger quantized model after the small one has a smoke test.

These are starting points, not laws. The same parameter count at a different quantization, context length, or runtime will use a different amount of memory. Watch the runner's reported memory and your system's pressure.

Rough machineStart here
8 GB unified or system memoryA small instruct model, heavily quantized. Keep the context short.
16 GBA 7B or 8B instruct model at a mid quantization such as Q4 or Q5.
32 GB or a discrete GPU with roomTry one size up only after the smaller model answers the smoke prompt.

Apple silicon uses unified memory. A discrete NVIDIA GPU uses its own memory, and the rest of the machine does not automatically extend it. CPU-only runs work and are slow. Slow is acceptable for a lesson. It is a product decision later.

Practice

Write your memory budget and the first model class you will try. Include the sentence you will use if it does not fit: which smaller model you fall back to.

Check

Why not start with the largest model you can find?

Show the answer

Because a model that does not fit does not run, and a model that barely fits leaves no room for context.

Lesson 04

Quantization trades precision for fit

Why it matters

The weights are stored with fewer bits. You measure whether your tasks still pass.

Try it: Memory fit

Lesson
04 of 07
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Change
How weights are stored
Label
Bit budget, not a grade
Different from
LoRA

Full-precision weights are large. Quantization stores those numbers in fewer bits so the model fits in memory and reads faster. GGUF is the file format llama.cpp and many local runners expect. You will see labels such as Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, and Q8_0. The digit is the bit budget. It is not a quality score.

A more aggressive quantization is smaller and more likely to damage reasoning, names, and tight formats. The only way to know is to run your fixture on two quantizations of the same model. If both pass, keep the smaller one. If the smaller one drops fields, step up or change models.

Words that get confused

Quantization changes how an existing model is stored. LoRA, in School 10, trains a small adapter. They are different tools and people mix the names in job posts. You should not.

Practice

In one paragraph, explain quantization to a teammate who thinks it means 'the model got smarter'. Include the measurement you would show them.

Check

What does Q4 tell you by itself?

Show the answer

That the weights were stored at about 4 bits. Not whether the model passes your tasks.

Lesson 05

Read the license before you ship a weight

Why it matters

Open weights are not one license. Some allow commercial use. Some restrict it. Some restrict use of the outputs for training.

Try it: Guardrail sandbox

Lesson
05 of 07
Time
9 min
Level
Practice
Read
The license on the weights
If unsure
Do not ship
Still separate
Rights in your data

A file you can download is not a file you can embed in a product. Model licenses differ: permissive licenses, licenses with an acceptable-use policy, and licenses that require a separate commercial grant above a size or revenue line. Read the license that shipped with the weights you pulled, not a blog summary of the family.

  • Record the model name, revision, and license name in the artifact.
  • If you are unsure whether your use is allowed, do not ship. Ask the licensor or pick a model whose terms you can explain.
  • Your prompts and your users' documents have their own rights. A model license does not clear those.

Practice

Choose one open model you might run. Write the license name and one thing that license does not automatically let you do. If you cannot find the license, write 'not found' and do not treat the model as cleared.

Check

Does downloadable mean you may sell a product that hides the model inside?

Show the answer

No. That depends on the license that came with those weights.

Lesson 06

Keep a smoke test you can rerun

Why it matters

After a reboot, prove the runner is up before you debug the prompt.

Try it: Proof record

Lesson
06 of 07
Time
8 min
Level
Practice
Same check
Every time
When
After a reboot, before the prompt
Artifact
Reply or the error

Half of 'the model got worse' is a runner that did not start, a disk that filled, or a different model tag than yesterday. A smoke test is cheaper than that confusion.

  1. Is the process up, and is it bound to localhost?
  2. Does the tag or file name match the model you think you are calling?
  3. Does a fixed 20-token prompt return a completion?
  4. Is there free disk for the context cache and logs?

Run this after install, after reboot, and after you pull a new model. Save the result with the date. Five lines is enough.

Practice

Write the four checks as commands or button-presses for your runner. Leave a blank line under each for the last result.

Check

What should you check before you rewrite a prompt that 'suddenly failed'?

Show the answer

That the runner is up and the model id matches the one in your last good artifact.

Lesson 07

Keep weights, prompts, and private data apart

Why it matters

Different files, different backups, different permissions.

Try it: Guardrail sandbox

Lesson
07 of 07
Time
9 min
Level
Core
Piles
Weights, prompts, data
Logs
Are a database
Permissions
Not your whole home

Weights are large, replaceable, and often re-downloadable. Prompts are small and are the thing you version. Private notes are neither weights nor prompts. Mixing them in one folder is how a zip of 'the lab' leaks a journal or how a cleanup script deletes the only copy of a prompt.

  • Weights live in the runner's store, which you do not commit.
  • Prompts and fixtures live in the project, without secrets.
  • Private corpora live outside the repo, with a path the code reads from configuration.
  • Logs that may contain prompt text are treated as private data, not as debug confetti.

Practice

Draw three boxes — weights, prompts, private data — and write the folder or setting you will use for each. Circle the one you will never commit.

Check

Which of the three belongs in git?

Show the answer

Prompts and fixtures that contain no secrets and no private corpus. Not weights. Not private notes.
